answer:
STRENGTHS: (1) Clear, real problem: cost-driven medication non-adherence among young adults with chronic conditions is well documented and emotionally resonant; the downstream cost of ER visits strengthens the value proposition. (2) Reasonable wedge: combining multi-source price comparison with budgeting and refill reminders, aimed at a specific, under-served and health-literacy-poor segment, is a plausible differentiation from generic discount-card apps. (3) Execution evidence for the stage: working prototype, incorporated entity, first outside users, and early qualitative feedback (users value price differences, want budgeting reminders). (4) Complementary, credible student team (public health/product, CS/build, business/partnerships) with domain exposure via a campus health center. (5) Founders are candid about unknowns (market size, unsigned referral deals, small sample, unmeasured retention), and the 12-month goal (prove savings and retention) is sensible and capital-efficient; the ~$75K ask is modest. (6) Clear campus-based initial distribution channel and logical secondary markets (campus health, employers, clinics).

WEAKNESSES: (1) Weak defensibility: the space is crowded with well-funded incumbents (discount card/coupon services, pharmacy and insurer apps, mail-order pharmacies) that can easily add budgeting or young-adult features; the stated differentiators are thin and mostly copyable. (2) Unproven economics: revenue depends on referral agreements with parties that have not been approached or signed, and referral fees per fill are typically small; the subscription willingness-to-pay among low-income young adults is unvalidated and likely low. No unit economics, CAC, LTV, or financial model. (3) Data dependency and risk: accurate, real-time pharmacy pricing is costly and hard to license; the prototype uses limited, partly sample data, so the core value (real savings) is not yet demonstrated. (4) Market sizing is vague ('several million', unrefined), and the target segment has low spending power, limiting monetization; secondary markets are untested. (5) Regulatory/privacy exposure: handling sensitive health and medication data (HIPAA-adjacent, state privacy laws, FTC health-data rules) is acknowledged as not yet understood; also potential conflicts of interest from referral-fee-driven recommendations. (6) Traction is minimal: a small, convenience sample of students, no measured savings, retention, or engagement; usage may be episodic (people check prices only at refill time), which challenges retention and subscription conversion. (7) Team limits: all students with no commercial healthcare, pharmacy-data, or regulatory experience; no formal advisors; team availability post-graduation is uncertain. (8) Go-to-market beyond the campus is unclear, and distribution into the broader 18-34 chronic-condition population has no validated channel.

OVERALL: A well-motivated, honestly framed, early-stage idea addressing a genuine problem with a sensible pilot plan, but with unvalidated monetization, weak moat against incumbents, data and compliance hurdles, and negligible traction. Interest is moderate-to-low as an investment today, appropriate for competition funding/mentorship rather than venture capital, with upside contingent on proving measurable savings, retention, and at least one signed referral or data partnership.
